slides.title: What a hallucination is
slides.summary: A hallucination is smooth, confident text that isn't true. It comes from how the model works, not from a bug in one place.
body: Ask a model who wrote a little-known paper, and it may give a name, a title and a year, all in a calm, expert tone. Every detail could be made up. That's a hallucination. Researchers also call it confabulation: a random, wrong answer that sounds right.

ul: Made-up facts: a person, date or number that never existed.
Fake sources: references, links, or code functions that don't exist.
Wrong summaries: a summary that disagrees with, or adds to, the document you gave the model.
Bad reasoning: steps that sound fine but hide a wrong sum or a jump in logic.

body: What they have in common is that they read smoothly. <mark>Smooth text is what a language model is best at, so how confident or polished an answer sounds tells you nothing about whether it's true.</mark>

body.note: Right and wrong answers come out in the same tone. You can't tell accuracy from style.

It doesn't only happen with tricky questions. It happens with everyday questions about things that are rarely written about, like small companies, little-known papers, and personal details about people.

body: The next slides cover four causes: what training rewards, what the data can teach, how models are tested, and how text is generated. Then we look at how to spot it and reduce it.

items.label: Made-up fact
items.sub: “The 2019 paper Rapid Gradient Shaping was written by Dr. Alan Whitmore of MIT.”

viz.html: All four examples are made up to illustrate. Each one would sound confident and correct.

figure.alt: Four causes lead to a fluent, confident answer whether or not the model knows: training rewards likely text, facts seen once can't be learned reliably, tests score a guess as no worse than "I don't know", and early wrong tokens become context the model stays consistent with. What helps: grounding in sources, rewarding "I don't know", tools for exact answers, checking outputs by asking several times, and honest product design.
figure.caption: The whole chapter on one page. Each cause and defence has its own slide.

slides.title: Cause 1: it predicts likely text, not true text
slides.summary: Training rewards likely next words and never checks facts. And the model always has to say something.
body: Remember the training goal from the Training chapter: predict the next token of real text. A guess is rewarded when it matches the real text, so the model gets very good at writing text that looks like real text. It only gets facts right as a side effect, when the real text happens to be true and consistent.

For a famous fact, the training text agrees with itself almost everywhere, so the model puts nearly all its probability on one answer. For an obscure fact, there's nothing consistent to learn, so the probability spreads over lots of names that all sound believable. Compare the two cases on the right.

Then, in both cases, generation does the same thing: pick a token based on the probabilities and move on. When one answer dominates, it's right almost every time. <mark>When the probability is spread out, the answer is basically random, but it's written in the same confident voice.</mark>

body.note: The final softmax always gives probabilities that add up to 1. There's no "nothing" option. Saying "I don't know" has to be learned as ordinary text, and plain next-token training gives the model little reason to learn it.
Likely and true match up when the training data has lots of consistent examples. They drift apart when the data is thin or contradicts itself.

code: next_id = sample(probs)   # peaked: the right answer. flat: an arbitrary one

blocks.html: One answer dominates. Picking from these gives the right answer nearly every time.
Prompt: “The author of the paper Rapid Gradient Shaping is Dr. ___” (no such paper exists)
The probability is spread out. Every name sounds fine, and whichever one is picked is stated as confidently as "Paris" would be. Numbers are made up for illustration.

slides.title: Cause 2: facts seen once can't be learned reliably
slides.summary: A model learns patterns from many examples. A random fact it saw only once, or never, gives it nothing to learn from.
body: Some knowledge has patterns the model can learn: spelling, grammar, how code is written. Millions of examples teach the pattern, and new cases follow it.

Other knowledge is random: someone's birthday, who wrote a paper, a phone number. No pattern predicts it. The model can only get it right if it saw that exact fact, and saw it often enough to remember it.

Count how many facts appear exactly once in the training data. Call that share the singleton rate. A 2025 OpenAI paper (Kalai et al., Why Language Models Hallucinate) argues that for random facts, a pretrained model will get at least about that share wrong. If 20% of birthdays appear only once, expect it to get at least about 20% of birthday questions wrong.
The idea: <mark>seeing something once isn't enough to tell a true fact from a believable alternative.</mark> Drag the slider to see how the minimum error changes.

body.note: This minimum applies to facts with no learnable pattern, in a model that has only been pretrained (the paper's setting). More data and bigger models lower the singleton rate, but real text always has a long tail of rare facts.
Hallucinating about rare facts doesn't mean the model is badly trained. It's a natural result of learning from a limited amount of text.

slides.title: Cause 3: tests reward guessing
slides.summary: Models are trained and tested on scores where a guess can earn points and "I don't know" earns nothing. So guessing becomes a habit.
body: Pretraining explains why hallucinations start. But why do they survive the later training stages? The same OpenAI paper points to how models are scored.

Most benchmarks mark like an exam with no penalty for wrong answers: right scores 1, wrong scores 0, and "I don't know" also scores 0. <mark>With those rules, guessing is never worse than not answering, so a model trained to score well learns to always answer, however unsure it is.</mark> As the paper puts it, models are trained to be good at taking tests.

Say the model is right with probability p when it guesses, and a wrong answer loses k points (zero in most benchmarks). Guessing scores p − (1 − p)·k on average. Not answering scores 0. So guessing only pays off when p > k / (1 + k). With k = 0, that's 0, so guessing always pays off.

The paper's suggested fix isn't a new hallucination test. It's to change how the existing, popular benchmarks score answers, so a confident mistake costs more than saying "I don't know". For example: answer only if you're at least 75% sure, and a wrong answer loses 3 points. Try the three scoring rules on the right.

body.note: Hallucination isn't only about what the model knows. It's also about what training and testing reward.

code: def expected_score(p, penalty):   # p = chance the guess is right
return guess, abstain          # guess wins when p > penalty / (1 + penalty)

slides.title: Cause 4: one wrong token leads to more
slides.summary: Text is written one token at a time with no backspace. So an early mistake becomes part of the text, and the model then tries to stay consistent with it.
body: Generation is a loop (see The big picture): each token is added to the text and the model continues from there. It never goes back and deletes a sentence. Once a wrong claim is written, it becomes evidence for what comes next.

Researchers call this hallucination snowballing (Zhang et al., 2023). They asked models questions where the first answer was often wrong, then watched them back it up with more false claims. When asked about those false claims separately, the same models could often spot the mistakes: GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2-70B-chat caught 67%, 87% and 94% of them. Changing the generation settings or prompting the model to think step by step didn't make the problem go away.

body.h: Other things that make it worse

ul: Random picking: with a high temperature or loose top-p, unlikely tokens get picked more often, and one odd token can send a sentence somewhere untrue (see Output & inference).
Long prompts: details buried in the middle of a very long prompt are remembered less reliably, so the model fills the gaps with believable guesses.
Out-of-date knowledge: the model doesn't know what has changed since its training cutoff, but it still answers as if it's up to date.

body.note: Check claims in a fresh request. A separate prompt asking "is this true?" isn't tied to the earlier text. That's why the models in the study could catch many mistakes they had just made.

slides.title: Inside the model: a "don't know" switch that misfires
slides.summary: Anthropic found that the model says "I can't answer" by default, and a feeling of familiarity switches that off. When the feeling is wrong, the model makes something up.
body: Researchers at Anthropic looked inside Claude 3.5 Haiku to see what happens when it's asked about people (Lindsey et al., 2025). What they found is the opposite of what you might expect: the model doesn't answer by default and sometimes stop itself.

ul: The default is to say no. A circuit that's always on makes the model say it doesn't have enough information to answer.
Familiarity switches it off. When the model recognises the subject (the example is Michael Jordan), "known person" signals turn off that default and the model answers.
An unknown name stays switched on. For a made-up name like Michael Batkin, nothing turns off the default, so the model says it doesn't know.

body: A misfire happens when the model recognises a name but knows nothing else about the person. The "known person" signal fires anyway and switches off the "I don't know" default. Now the model has to answer, so it writes something believable but untrue. In one experiment, the team made the model hallucinate on purpose by artificially boosting those "I know this" signals.

body.note: The model isn't being careless. A feeling of recognition overrides a "don't know" switch that was otherwise working fine.

This is one mechanism, in one model, for questions about people. Other hallucinations have other causes, and other models may work differently. <mark>What it shows is that recognising a topic and actually knowing the answer are two separate signals, and they can disagree.</mark>

blocks.html: Question about Michael Batkin (not a known person)
A name the model has seen, but knows nothing else about

viz.html: Simplified from Anthropic's published findings for Claude 3.5 Haiku. Real circuits involve many more signals.

slides.title: Spotting hallucinations: ask more than once
slides.summary: If a model really knows the answer, it gives the same answer every time. If it's guessing, the answers are all over the place.
body: It's hard to tell how sure a model is from one answer, because smooth writing hides it. <mark>But you can ask the same question several times and compare the answers.</mark>

Semantic entropy (Farquhar et al., Nature, 2024) does exactly that. Get several answers, group the ones that mean the same thing, and measure how spread out the groups are. Answers that agree give a low score (the model probably knows). Answers that are all different give a high score (it's probably making it up).
Grouping by meaning is important: "Paris" and "It's Paris." are the same answer even though the words differ. In the paper, a second language model decides whether two answers mean the same thing.

The method doesn't need any labelled examples of hallucinations, and in the paper's tests it did better than simpler methods. The downside is that it needs several answers per question plus the grouping step, so it's used where reliability is worth the extra cost.

ul: Check outside the model: run the code, look up the reference, check the number in a database.
A separate fact-check: ask in a fresh prompt whether a claim is true, as in the snowballing study.
A second model as reviewer: have another model flag claims that the sources don't back up.

code: groups = cluster_by_meaning(answers)   # a second model judges 'same meaning?'
p = [len(g) / len(answers) for g in groups]
entropy = -sum(x * log(x) for x in p)  # high means the model is guessing

All five answers mean the same thing. The model is consistent, so the answer is more likely to be right.

slides.title: Reducing hallucinations: where each defence fits
slides.summary: Hallucination can't be removed completely, so assistants make it less likely, check what the model writes, and let it say "I don't know".
body: The causes come from statistics and from what training rewards, so no single fix gets rid of hallucination. Real systems stack defences, and you've already met most of these layers in Assistant architecture:

ul: Give the model the facts. Search and retrieval (RAG) put real source text in front of the model, so it reads the answer instead of remembering it. It can still misread a source, which is why good answers point to the exact passages.
Make "I don't know" a good answer. Reward the model in training for admitting when it's unsure, use scoring that punishes confident mistakes, and tell the model it's fine to say when it doesn't know.
Use tools for exact answers. A calculator for maths, a code runner for code, a database for records.
Check the output. Consistency checks like semantic entropy, checking references, or a second model reviewing claims.
Design the product honestly. Show sources, mark when the model is unsure, and have a person check anything important, like medical, legal or financial answers.

body.note: If you're building an app: base answers on your own data, require references, and test with questions you know the answers to, including ones the model should refuse. Measure how often it hallucinates on your own data, not just on public benchmarks.

Grounding reduces hallucination but doesn't get rid of it. Models can still misquote a source or read too much into it. <mark>Treat a reference as a way to check an answer, not as proof it's right.</mark>

items.label: Ground in sources
items.sub: Search and retrieval put real text in front of the model.

items.label: Train for honesty
items.sub: Reward honest "I don't know"; fix the scoring.

items.label: Detect and flag
items.sub: Ask several times and compare the meanings.

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.summary: You've seen the model and the system around it. Building both yourself is the best way to make it stick.
body: You've now seen every part of a modern LLM, and the system that turns it into an assistant. As an engineer, the best way to make it stick is to build both yourself.

ul: Andrej Karpathy, "Let's build GPT" and nanoGPT: a GPT in a few hundred lines of PyTorch.
"Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017): the original paper. You'll be able to follow it after this course.
Jay Alammar, "The Illustrated Transformer": more diagrams of the same ideas.
Anthropic's constitution and system prompt release notes, and OpenAI's Model Spec: how AI companies write down how their models should behave.
"The Instruction Hierarchy" (Wallace et al., 2024) and "Defeating Prompt Injections by Design" (CaMeL, 2025).
The MCP specification and Simon Willison's writing on prompt injection.
"Why Language Models Hallucinate" (Kalai et al., OpenAI, 2025) and "How Language Model Hallucinations Can Snowball" (Zhang et al., 2023).
Anthropic, "Tracing the thoughts of a large language model" (2025) and "Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy" (Farquhar et al., Nature, 2024).

body: Three good exercises. First, build the 4-token attention example from the Attention chapter in plain Java or TypeScript, and check your numbers match. Second, write the short tool loop from Assistant architecture against a real API, and add a permission check before each tool call. Third, pick one question you know the answer to and one about a little-known person. Ask each five times at temperature 1 and compare how much the answers change.
